nodes.summary: For every predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ and every red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, $p$ holds at every key of $t$ if and only if $p$ holds at every key of the binary search tree obtained from $t$ by erasing colors. This holds by definition.
nodes.title: All keys of a red-black tree via its color erasure

nodes.summary: For every predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ and every red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, $p$ holds at every key of $t$ if and only if $p(x)$ holds for every $x \in \alpha$ that is a (structural) member of $t$.
nodes.title: All keys versus members of a red-black tree

nodes.summary: For a predicate $p$ on $\alpha$ and a red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$, $p$ holds at every key of $t$ when $p$ holds at every key of the binary search tree obtained from $t$ by erasing colors.
nodes.title: Predicate holding at every key of a red-black tree

nodes.summary: A red-black tree satisfies the relaxed red invariant when it is empty, or when its left and right subtrees both satisfy the red invariant (no red node has a red child). The root itself is unconstrained, so a red root may have a red child.
nodes.title: Red invariant away from the root

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a color, $L$ a tree whose root may be double black, $k$ a key and $R$ a red-black tree. If $L$ is a genuine red-black tree, the result is the genuine node with color $c$, left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$. Otherwise the double black of $L$ is absorbed first: a double-black empty tree becomes the empty tree, and a double-black node becomes the black node with the same children and key. The…
nodes.title: Rebalancing after deletion from the left subtree

nodes.summary: Let $c$ be a color, $L$ a red-black tree, $k$ a key and $R$ a tree whose root may be double black. If $R$ is a genuine red-black tree, the result is the genuine node with color $c$, left subtree $L$, key $k$ and right subtree $R$. Otherwise the double black of $R$ is absorbed first: a double-black empty tree becomes the empty tree, and a double-black node becomes the black node with the same children and key. The…
nodes.title: Rebalancing after deletion from the right subtree

nodes.summary: Given a color $c$, red-black trees $l$ and $r$, and a key $k$, rebalancing produces a tree as follows. Suppose $c$ is black and one of these configurations occurs, taking the first that applies: $l$ is a red node with a red left child; $l$ is a red node with a red right child; $r$ is a red node with a red left child; $r$ is a red node with a red right child. The black root and the two red nodes then hold three keys…
nodes.title: Okasaki's rebalancing

nodes.summary: A tree whose root may be double black is balanced when it is a genuine red-black tree that is balanced, when it is the double-black empty tree, or when it is a double-black node whose left and right subtrees are both balanced and have the same black height.
nodes.title: Black-height balance of a possibly double-black tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, and $T$ a valid red-black tree over $\alpha$. Then the tree obtained from $T$ by double-black deletion of $x$ is balanced.
nodes.title: Double-black deletion keeps a valid tree balanced

nodes.summary: For every linearly ordered type of keys, every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, with no hypothesis on $t$, the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding is black-height balanced.
nodes.title: Deletion by rebuilding is black-height balanced

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. If a red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$ is balanced (every root-to-leaf path contains the same number of black nodes), then for every $x \in \alpha$ the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is balanced.
nodes.title: Red-black insertion preserves black-height balance

nodes.summary: A red-black tree is balanced when every root-to-leaf path contains the same number of black nodes. Recursively: the empty tree is balanced, and a node is balanced when both of its subtrees are balanced and have the same black height (the number of black nodes on the leftmost root-to-leaf path, counting the leaf).
nodes.title: Black-height balanced red-black tree

nodes.summary: A tree with a possibly double-black root over a type $\alpha$ is one of the following: a genuine red-black tree over $\alpha$; the double-black empty tree; or a double-black node consisting of a left subtree, a key in $\alpha$ and a right subtree, where both subtrees are genuine red-black trees. Hence a double black can occur only at the root.
nodes.title: Trees with a possibly double-black root

nodes.summary: An extended color is one of three values: red, black or double black.
nodes.title: Extended root colors

nodes.summary: The black height of a genuine red-black tree is its usual black height. The double-black empty tree has black height $2$, and a double-black node with left subtree $L$ has black height $h(L) + 2$, where $h(L)$ is the usual black height of $L$. Thus a double-black root counts as two black nodes, where the usual black height counts the empty tree as one.
nodes.title: Black height of a possibly double-black tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$, $T$ a valid red-black tree over $\alpha$, and $T'$ the tree obtained from $T$ by double-black deletion of $x$. Then the black height of $T'$ either equals the black height of $T$ or is one less than it.
nodes.title: Black height after double-black deletion

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every red-black tree $t$ with keys in $\alpha$ and every $x \in \alpha$, the black height of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ equals either the black height of $t$ or the black height of $t$ plus one.
nodes.title: Insertion raises the black height by at most one

nodes.summary: The black height of a red-black tree is the number of black nodes on its leftmost root-to-leaf path, counting the empty leaf as one black node: the empty tree has black height $1$, a red node has the black height of its left subtree, and a black node has the black height of its left subtree plus $1$.
nodes.title: Black height

nodes.summary: Blackening sends a tree whose root may be double black to a genuine red-black tree by changing only its root: a genuine tree has its root recolored black (the empty tree stays empty), the double-black empty tree becomes the empty tree, and a double-black node becomes the black node with the same subtrees and key.
nodes.title: Absorbing a double-black root

nodes.summary: The extended color of a tree whose root may be double black is the color of its root, red or black, when it is a genuine red-black tree, where the empty tree counts as black; it is double black for the double-black empty tree and for every double-black node.
nodes.title: Extended root color

nodes.summary: For every key $x$ of a linearly ordered type and every red-black tree $t$, valid or not, the root of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is black, where the empty tree counts as black.
nodes.title: Double-black deletion leaves a black root

nodes.summary: For every linearly ordered type of keys, every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, with no hypothesis on $t$, the root of the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding is black, where the empty tree counts as having a black root.
nodes.title: Deletion by rebuilding gives a black root

nodes.summary: The root color of a red-black tree is the color of its root node; the empty tree has root color black.
nodes.title: Root color

nodes.summary: The colors of red-black tree nodes are the two values red and black.
nodes.title: Red-black node colors

nodes.summary: Let $t$ be a red-black tree over a linearly ordered type that is ordered (every left key is smaller and every right key larger, recursively). Then for every key $x$, the search for $x$ in $t$ returns true if and only if $x$ is a key of some node of $t$.
nodes.title: Search in an ordered red-black tree is correct

nodes.summary: Searching a red-black tree over a linearly ordered type for a key $x$ returns a Boolean, ignoring colors: the empty tree gives false, and at a node with key $k$ the search continues in the left subtree if $x < k$, continues in the right subtree if $k < x$, and returns true otherwise.
nodes.title: Search in a red-black tree

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type, deleting $x$ from a red-black tree returns a tree whose root may be double black, by recursion on the tree. The empty tree gives the empty tree. At a node of color $c$ with left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$: if $x < k$, the result is the left reassembly of color $c$, the deletion of $x$ from $l$, key $k$ and $r$; if $k < x$, it is the right reassembly of color…
nodes.title: Double-black deletion

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type, unbalanced deletion of $x$ from a red-black tree is defined by recursion on the tree. The empty tree stays empty. At a node with color $c$, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$: if $x < k$, the result is the node with color $c$, left subtree the unbalanced deletion of $x$ from $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$; if $k < x$, it is the node with color $c$, left…
nodes.title: Unbalanced red-black tree deletion

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type and a red-black tree $t$, deleting $x$ from $t$ runs the double-black deletion of $x$ from $t$, which returns a tree whose root may be double black, and then absorbs a remaining double black at the root and recolors the root black.
nodes.title: Red-black tree deletion by the double-black method

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type and a red-black tree $t$, deleting $x$ from $t$ by rebuilding first forms the unbalanced deletion of $x$ from $t$, then rebalances it: starting from the empty tree, it inserts the keys of the inorder traversal of that tree one at a time, from the last key to the first.
nodes.title: Red-black tree deletion by rebuilding

nodes.summary: For every red-black tree $t$, the color erasure of the tree obtained from $t$ by recoloring its root black (the empty tree is left unchanged) equals the color erasure of $t$.
nodes.title: Recoloring the root black does not change the color erasure

nodes.summary: The color erasure of a red-black tree is the binary tree obtained by forgetting the node colors: the empty tree goes to the empty binary tree, and a node with key $k$ and subtrees $l$ and $r$ goes to the binary-tree node with key $k$ whose subtrees are the color erasures of $l$ and $r$.
nodes.title: Color erasure

nodes.summary: Write $\mathrm{R}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ for red and black, and $N(c, T, y, T')$ for the node of color $c$ with left subtree $T$, key $y$ and right subtree $T'$. Given a color $c$, a tree $D$, a key $k$ and a tree $S$, the left repair returns a tree whose root may be double black, by the first case that applies. If $S = N(\mathrm{B}, T_1, y, N(\mathrm{R}, T_2, z, T_3))$ or, failing that,…
nodes.title: Left repair after double-black deletion

nodes.summary: Write $\mathrm{R}$ and $\mathrm{B}$ for red and black, and $N(c, T, y, T')$ for the node of color $c$ with left subtree $T$, key $y$ and right subtree $T'$. Given a color $c$, a tree $S$, a key $k$ and a tree $D$, the right repair returns a tree whose root may be double black, by the first case that applies. If $S = N(\mathrm{B}, N(\mathrm{R}, T_1, y, T_2), z, T_3)$ or, failing that,…
nodes.title: Right repair after double-black deletion

nodes.summary: The red-black tree built from a list over a linearly ordered type inserts the elements of the list into the empty tree from right to left: the empty list gives the empty tree, and a list with head $x$ and tail $xs$ gives the insertion of $x$ into the tree built from $xs$.
nodes.title: Red-black tree from a list

nodes.summary: Add one black to the root of a red-black tree, producing a tree whose root may be double black: the empty tree becomes the double-black empty tree, a red root becomes black, and a black root becomes double black.
nodes.title: Adding a black to the root

nodes.summary: For a red-black tree $t$ and a list $s$, this is the accumulator form of the binary-search-tree inorder traversal applied to the color erasure of $t$: for the empty tree it returns $s$, and for a node with key $k$ and subtrees $l$ and $r$ it returns the result for $l$ with suffix the list $k$ followed by $u$, where $u$ is the result for $r$ with suffix $s$.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal onto a suffix

nodes.summary: The inorder traversal of a red-black tree whose root may be double black ignores the double-black mark: a genuine tree gives its inorder traversal, the double-black empty tree gives the empty list, and a double-black node with left child $l$, key $k$ and right child $r$ gives the inorder traversal of $l$, followed by $k$, followed by the inorder traversal of $r$.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal of a possibly double-black tree

nodes.summary: For a key $x$ of a linearly ordered type and an ordered red-black tree $t$, the inorder traversal of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is the inorder traversal of $t$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed (unchanged if $x$ does not occur).
nodes.title: Double-black deletion erases the key from the inorder traversal

nodes.summary: Let $x$ be a key of a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be an ordered red-black tree. Then the inorder traversal of the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding is the inorder traversal of $t$ with the first occurrence of $x$ removed (it is unchanged if $x$ does not occur).
nodes.title: Inorder traversal after deletion by rebuilding

nodes.summary: For every red-black tree $t$, the inorder traversal of $t$ equals the binary-search-tree inorder traversal of the color erasure of $t$; this holds by definition.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal ignores colors

nodes.summary: For red-black trees $t$ and $s$ with keys of any type, the inorder traversal of the splice of $t$ with $s$ is the inorder traversal of $t$ followed by the inorder traversal of $s$.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal of a splice

nodes.summary: For a red-black tree $t$ over a linearly ordered type that is ordered (every left key is smaller and every right key larger, recursively), the inorder traversal of $t$ contains no key twice.
nodes.title: Ordered red-black trees have duplicate-free inorder traversals

nodes.summary: The inorder traversal of a red-black tree $t$ is the binary-search-tree inorder traversal of the color erasure of $t$, computed in linear time with an accumulator starting from the empty list. It lists the keys of $t$ from left to right: the empty tree gives the empty list, and a node with key $k$ and subtrees $l$ and $r$ gives the traversal of $l$, then $k$, then the traversal of $r$.
nodes.title: Inorder traversal of a red-black tree

nodes.summary: For keys from a linearly ordered type, the unchecked insertion of $x$ into a red-black tree is defined by recursion on the tree. Inserting $x$ into the empty tree gives a red node with key $x$ and two empty subtrees. Inserting $x$ into a node with color $c$, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$ gives: if $x < k$, Okasaki's rebalancing of color $c$, left subtree the insertion of $x$ into $l$, key $k$ and…
nodes.title: Unchecked red-black insertion

nodes.summary: For keys from a linearly ordered type, inserting $x$ into a red-black tree $t$ gives the unchecked insertion of $x$ into $t$ with its root recolored black.
nodes.title: Red-black tree insertion

nodes.summary: The splice of a red-black tree $t$ with a red-black tree $s$ is defined by recursion on $t$. The splice of the empty tree with $s$ is $s$. The splice of the node with color $c$, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$ with $s$ is the node with color $c$, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree the splice of $r$ with $s$.
nodes.title: Splicing two red-black trees

nodes.summary: Recoloring the root of a red-black tree black leaves the empty tree unchanged and turns a node with any color, left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$ into the black node with left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$.
nodes.title: Blackening the root

nodes.summary: For keys $x$ and $y$ of a linearly ordered type and an ordered red-black tree $t$, $y$ is a key of the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method if and only if $y$ is a key of $t$ and $y \ne x$.
nodes.title: Keys after double-black deletion

nodes.summary: Let $x$ and $y$ be keys of a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be an ordered red-black tree. Then $y$ belongs to the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding if and only if $y$ belongs to $t$ and $y \ne x$.
nodes.title: Membership after deletion by rebuilding

nodes.summary: For every red-black tree $t$ and every $x$, $x$ is a member of $t$ if and only if $x$ is a member of the binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its colors.
nodes.title: Red-black membership is membership in the underlying binary tree

nodes.summary: For keys from a linearly ordered type and every list $xs$, a key $x$ is a member of the red-black tree built from $xs$ by successive insertion if and only if $x$ occurs in $xs$.
nodes.title: Membership in a red-black tree built from a list

nodes.summary: For every red-black tree $t$ and every $x$, $x$ occurs in the inorder traversal of $t$ if and only if $x$ is a member of $t$.
nodes.title: Membership in the inorder traversal of a red-black tree

nodes.summary: For keys from a linearly ordered type, a key $y$ is a member of the red-black tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ if and only if $y = x$ or $y$ is a member of $t$.
nodes.title: Membership after insertion into a red-black tree

nodes.summary: For red-black trees $t$ and $s$ with keys of any type, a key $x$ belongs to the splice of $t$ with $s$ if and only if $x$ belongs to $t$ or $x$ belongs to $s$.
nodes.title: Membership in a splice

nodes.summary: An element $x$ is a member of a red-black tree $t$ when $x$ is a member of the binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its colors, that is, when $x$ equals the key of some node of $t$.
nodes.title: Membership in a red-black tree

nodes.summary: For a red-black tree $t$ over a type $\alpha$, the leftmost key of $t$ is either a key in $\alpha$ or undefined. It is undefined when $t$ is empty. When $t$ is a node, of either color, with left subtree $l$ and key $k$, it is the leftmost key of $l$ if that is defined, and $k$ otherwise. Hence the leftmost key is defined exactly when $t$ is nonempty.
nodes.title: Leftmost key of a red-black tree

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered, that is, at every node all keys of the left subtree are strictly smaller and all keys of the right subtree are strictly larger than the node's key. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the key $x$ does not occur in the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method.
nodes.title: The deleted key is absent after double-black deletion

nodes.summary: Let $x$ be a key of a linearly ordered type and let $t$ be an ordered red-black tree. Then $x$ does not belong to the tree obtained from $t$ by deleting $x$ by rebuilding.
nodes.title: The deleted key is absent after deletion by rebuilding

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered, that is, at every node all keys of the left subtree are strictly smaller and all keys of the right subtree are strictly larger than the node's key. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is again ordered.
nodes.title: Double-black deletion preserves the search-tree order

nodes.summary: For every linearly ordered key type, every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ is ordered: at every node, all keys in the left subtree are strictly smaller than the node's key and all keys in the right subtree are strictly larger. No hypothesis on $t$ is needed.
nodes.title: Red-black deletion yields an ordered tree

nodes.summary: For keys with a relation $<$, a red-black tree $t$ is ordered if and only if the binary tree obtained from $t$ by erasing its colors is an ordered binary search tree.
nodes.title: A red-black tree is ordered exactly when its underlying binary tree is

nodes.summary: For keys from a linearly ordered type, if a red-black tree $t$ is ordered, then every entry of the inorder traversal of $t$ is strictly smaller than every later entry.
nodes.title: The inorder traversal of an ordered red-black tree is strictly increasing

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$ a key, and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$. If $t$ is ordered (at every node with key $k$, every key in the left subtree is less than $k$ and every key in the right subtree is greater than $k$), then the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is ordered.
nodes.title: Red-black insertion preserves the search-tree order

nodes.summary: Let $<$ be a relation on the keys, and let $L$ and $R$ be red-black trees that are ordered for $<$ such that $a < b$ for every key $a$ of $L$ and every key $b$ of $R$. Then the join of $L$ and $R$, obtained by putting $R$ in place of the empty right subtree of the rightmost node of $L$ (or $R$ itself if $L$ is empty) and keeping all colors, is ordered.
nodes.title: Joining separated ordered trees preserves order

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. A red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ is ordered when, at every node with key $k$, every key $y$ in the left subtree satisfies $y < k$ and every key $z$ in the right subtree satisfies $k < z$.
nodes.title: Ordered red-black tree

nodes.summary: For a linearly ordered key type, the rebuild of a red-black tree $t$ is the tree obtained from the empty tree by inserting the keys of the inorder traversal of $t$ one at a time with Okasaki insertion, starting from the last key.
nodes.title: Rebuilding a red-black tree from its keys

nodes.summary: A tree whose root may be double black satisfies the red invariant in the following cases: a genuine red-black tree satisfies it when it satisfies the usual red invariant (no red node has a red child); the double-black empty tree always satisfies it; and a double-black node with left subtree $l$ and right subtree $r$ satisfies it when both $l$ and $r$ satisfy the usual red invariant.
nodes.title: Red invariant for trees with a possibly double-black root

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $t$ a valid red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$: it is ordered, satisfies the red invariant, is black-height balanced, and has a black root. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method satisfies the red invariant: no red node has a red child.
nodes.title: Double-black deletion from a valid tree keeps the red invariant

nodes.summary: For every linearly ordered key type, every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ satisfies the red invariant: no red node has a red child. No hypothesis on $t$ is needed.
nodes.title: Red-black deletion yields a tree with no red-red edge

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$ a key, and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$. If no red node of $t$ has a red child, then no red node of the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ has a red child.
nodes.title: Red-black insertion preserves the red property

nodes.summary: A red-black tree satisfies the red property when no red node has a red child, where empty subtrees count as black.
nodes.title: Red property of red-black trees

nodes.summary: For a red-black tree $t$, this is the tree obtained from $t$ by coloring its root black: the empty tree stays empty, and a node with left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$, of either color, becomes the black node with left subtree $l$, key $k$ and right subtree $r$.
nodes.title: Recoloring the root black

nodes.summary: A red-black tree with keys in a type $\alpha$ is either empty or a node consisting of a color (red or black), a left subtree, a key in $\alpha$, and a right subtree.
nodes.title: Red-black tree data type

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered, satisfies the red invariant (no red node has a red child), and is black-height balanced (all root-to-leaf paths contain the same number of black nodes). Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is a valid red-black tree.
nodes.title: Double-black deletion yields a valid tree from the structural invariants

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $t$ a valid red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$: it is ordered, satisfies the red invariant, is black-height balanced, and has a black root. Then for every $x \in \alpha$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ by the double-black method is again a valid red-black tree.
nodes.title: Double-black deletion preserves validity

nodes.summary: For every linearly ordered key type, every key $x$ and every red-black tree $t$, the tree obtained by deleting $x$ from $t$ is a valid red-black tree: it is ordered, no red node has a red child, every root-to-leaf path contains the same number of black nodes, and its root is black (the empty tree counts as black). No hypothesis on $t$ is needed.
nodes.title: Red-black deletion yields a valid red-black tree

nodes.summary: For every type $\alpha$ with a relation $<$, the empty red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ is a valid red-black tree.
nodes.title: The empty red-black tree is valid

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type. For every list $l$ of elements of $\alpha$, the red-black tree obtained from the empty tree by inserting the elements of $l$ one at a time, from the last to the first, is valid.
nodes.title: Red-black trees built from a list are valid

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type, $x \in \alpha$ a key, and $t$ a red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ that is ordered, satisfies the red property (no red node has a red child), and is balanced (every root-to-leaf path contains the same number of black nodes). Then the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is valid.
nodes.title: Red-black insertion yields a valid tree from the invariants

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linearly ordered type and $x \in \alpha$. If $t$ is a valid red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$, then the tree obtained by inserting $x$ into $t$ is also valid.
nodes.title: Red-black insertion preserves validity

nodes.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a type with a relation $<$. A red-black tree with keys in $\alpha$ is valid when it is ordered, satisfies the red property (no red node has a red child), is balanced (every root-to-leaf path contains the same number of black nodes), and its root is black, where the empty tree counts as black.
nodes.title: Valid red-black tree
Computer Science

can_prove.label: ready to prove
can_prove.meaning: Statement is in Lean and nothing it needs is blocked, so the proof can start.

can_state.label: ready to state
can_state.meaning: Everything its statement uses is in Lean, so the statement can be written in Lean.

conditional.label: conditionally proved
conditional.meaning: Proof compiles, but rests on an open statement without a recorded Lean proof.

fully_proved.label: fully proved
fully_proved.meaning: Proved, and every prerequisite is fully proved too.

inventory_checked.label: inventory checked
inventory_checked.meaning: Module inventory checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

inventory_pending.label: inventory pending
inventory_pending.meaning: Module inventory not yet checked in full; it records inspection, not a mathematical proof.

not_ready.label: not ready
not_ready.meaning: Needs more blueprint work before it can be attempted.

proved.label: proved
proved.meaning: Proof compiles, but something it rests on is not finished.

stated.label: statement formalized
stated.meaning: Statement is in Lean; the proof is not.
